claim: The Fluc family of F− ion channels protects prokaryotes and lower eukaryotes from the toxicity of environmental F−.
source: The Fluc family of F− ion channels protects prokaryotes and lower eukaryotes from the toxicity of environmental F−.
evidence: This is a statement about the biological function of Fluc channels, drawing from established scientific knowledge about these channels.

claim: In bacteria, Fluc channels are built as dual-topology dimers whereby the two subunits assemble in antiparallel transmembrane orientation.
source: In bacteria, these channels are built as dual-topology dimers whereby the two subunits assemble in antiparallel transmembrane orientation.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to prior structural and biochemical work on Fluc channels.

claim: Recent crystal structures suggested that Fluc channels contain two separate ion-conduction pathways, each with two F− binding sites.
source: Recent crystal structures suggested that Fluc channels contain two separate ion-conduction pathways, each with two F− binding sites, but no functional correlates of this unusual architecture have been reported.
evidence: This claim references prior crystallographic studies that proposed the dual-pathway architecture.

claim: No functional correlates of the dual-pathway architecture have been reported prior to this study.
source: Recent crystal structures suggested that Fluc channels contain two separate ion-conduction pathways, each with two F− binding sites, but no functional correlates of this unusual architecture have been reported.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature prior to the current work.

claim: Substitution of each phenylalanine specifically extinguishes its associated F− binding site in crystal structures.
source: Substitution of each phenylalanine specifically extinguishes its associated F− binding site in crystal structures and concomitantly inhibits F− permeation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structures of F80I and F83I mutants presented in the manuscript.

claim: Substitution of each phenylalanine concomitantly inhibits F− permeation.
source: Substitution of each phenylalanine specifically extinguishes its associated F− binding site in crystal structures and concomitantly inhibits F− permeation.
evidence: This is supported by the F− flux assays showing loss of transport activity in the mutants.

claim: Each pore can be separately inactivated without blocking F− conduction through its symmetry-related twin.
source: Functional analysis of concatemeric channels, which permit mutagenic manipulation of individual pores, show that each pore can be separately inactivated without blocking F− conduction through its symmetry-related twin.
evidence: This is supported by the flux and single-channel data from concatemeric constructs with single-pore mutations.

claim: The results strongly support dual-pathway architecture of Fluc channels.
source: The results strongly support dual-pathway architecture of Fluc channels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: F− has been generally considered an irrelevant nonparticipant in membrane biology.
source: The F− ion, ubiquitous in the aqueous biosphere since the dawn of life, has been generally considered an irrelevant nonparticipant in membrane biology.
evidence: This reflects the historical view in the field prior to recent discoveries.

claim: The discovery of F−-specific riboswitches in many bacterial genomes upended the view that F− is irrelevant in membrane biology.
source: This view was recently upended by the discovery of F−-specific riboswitches in many bacterial genomes (Baker et al., 2012), a breakthrough that over the past few years has revealed F−-transporting membrane proteins underpinning a widespread microbial physiology of resistance to environmental F− toxicity (Baker et al., 2012; Stockbridge et al., 2012; Li S et al., 2013; Ji et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the riboswitch discovery and subsequent work on F− transport proteins.

claim: F−-transporting membrane proteins underpin a widespread microbial physiology of resistance to environmental F− toxicity.
source: This view was recently upended by the discovery of F−-specific riboswitches in many bacterial genomes (Baker et al., 2012), a breakthrough that over the past few years has revealed F−-transporting membrane proteins underpinning a widespread microbial physiology of resistance to environmental F− toxicity (Baker et al., 2012; Stockbridge et al., 2012; Li S et al., 2013; Ji et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on F− transport and resistance.

claim: F− exporters fall into two phylogenetically unrelated classes: energy-consuming anion transporters of the CLC superfamily and electrodiffusive, F−-specific ion channels of the Fluc family.
source: These F− exporters fall into two phylogenetically unrelated classes: energy-consuming anion transporters of the CLC superfamily (Stockbridge et al., 2012; Brammer et al., 2014), and electrodiffusive, F−-specific ion channels of the Fluc family (Stockbridge et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies characterizing these two classes of F− exporters.

claim: CLC proteins have been studied for decades.
source: While CLC proteins have been studied for decades (Miller, 2015), Flucs represent a novel and idiosyncratic class of ion channels.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and reflects established knowledge in the field.

claim: Flucs represent a novel and idiosyncratic class of ion channels.
source: While CLC proteins have been studied for decades (Miller, 2015), Flucs represent a novel and idiosyncratic class of ion channels.
evidence: This is a characterization based on the recent discovery and unique properties of Fluc channels.

claim: Bacterial Fluc channels assemble as dimers of small subunits (120–130 residues, 4 transmembrane helices) arranged in antiparallel transmembrane topology.
source: Bacterial Fluc channels assemble as dimers of small subunits (120–130 residues, 4 transmembrane helices) arranged in antiparallel transmembrane topology.
evidence: This is supported by prior biochemical and structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Dual-topology architecture of Fluc channels was originally inferred from biochemical and electrophysiological behavior.
source: This dual-topology architecture, originally inferred from biochemical and electrophysiological behavior (Stockbridge et al., 2013; Stockbridge et al., 2014), was recently observed in crystal structures of two homodimeric Fluc homologues (Stockbridge et al., 2015), as depicted in Figure 1a.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior functional studies.

claim: Dual-topology architecture was recently observed in crystal structures of two homodimeric Fluc homologues.
source: This dual-topology architecture, originally inferred from biochemical and electrophysiological behavior (Stockbridge et al., 2013; Stockbridge et al., 2014), was recently observed in crystal structures of two homodimeric Fluc homologues (Stockbridge et al., 2015), as depicted in Figure 1a.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior structural work and reference to Figure 1a showing the structure.

claim: The hourglass-shaped channel is complexed with two 'monobody' crystallization chaperones, which plug each of the wide vestibules facing the two aqueous solutions.
source: The hourglass-shaped channel is complexed with two 'monobody' crystallization chaperones, which plug each of the wide vestibules facing the two aqueous solutions. (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Monobodies are ~10 kDa engineered proteins.
source: These ~10 kDa engineered monobodies are also high-affinity channel blockers whose long-lived block-times are readily observed in single-channel recordings (Stockbridge et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the monobodies supported by citation.

claim: Monobodies are high-affinity channel blockers whose long-lived block-times are readily observed in single-channel recordings.
source: These ~10 kDa engineered monobodies are also high-affinity channel blockers whose long-lived block-times are readily observed in single-channel recordings (Stockbridge et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and by single-channel data in the current manuscript.

claim: Crystal structures suggested that Flucs contain two pores running along the sides of the complex, with each pore built by residues from both subunits.
source: The structures suggested an additional surprising feature of Fluc proteins: double-barreled architecture. In contrast to most ion channels, in which a single ion-permeation pore spans the membrane along a central axis, Flucs were proposed to contain two pores running along the sides of the complex, with each pore built by residues from both subunits (Stockbridge et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on prior structural analysis cited in the manuscript.

claim: This double-barreled architecture inference is unaccompanied by any functional behavior that would support or refute this picture.
source: However, this is a crystallographically 'dry' inference based on structural results alone, unaccompanied by any functional behavior that would add mechanistic vitality to support or refute this otherwise unprecedented picture.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of evidence prior to the current study.

claim: The crevices housing the anion densities are too narrow to show themselves at 2.1–2.6 Å resolution as clearly delineated aqueous pores traversing the protein.
source: An additional crystallographic ambiguity is that the crevices housing the anion densities are too narrow to show themselves at 2.1–2.6 Å resolution as clearly delineated aqueous pores traversing the protein.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the crystallographic data.

claim: The argument for dual-pathway construction is not yet consummated and calls for tests based on functional properties of the pores manipulated individually.
source: For these reasons, we consider that the argument for dual-pathway construction is not yet consummated; it calls for tests based on functional properties of the pores manipulated individually.
evidence: This is a statement of the motivation for the current study.

claim: By solving crystal structures of ion-permeation mutants of a bacterial Fluc channel and analyzing the behavior of fused-dimer constructs, the authors unambiguously establish the two-pore character of Fluc channels.
source: By solving crystal structures of ion-permeation mutants of a bacterial Fluc channel and analyzing the behavior of fused-dimer constructs, we now unambiguously establish the two-pore character of Fluc channels.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: All experiments employ the previously described 'Ec2' Fluc homologue from an E. coli virulence plasmid.
source: All experiments here employ the previously described 'Ec2' Fluc homologue from an E. coli virulence plasmid (Stockbridge et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental system used, supported by citation.

claim: The homodimeric channel's symmetric, dual-topology structure demands that the pores adopt antiparallel orientations.
source: The homodimeric channel's symmetric, dual-topology structure demands that the pores adopt antiparallel orientations and that the two chemically distinct F− ions in one pore, designated F1− and F2−, are mirrored symmetrically in the other.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the structural symmetry of the channel.

claim: The two chemically distinct F− ions in one pore, designated F1− and F2−, are mirrored symmetrically in the other pore.
source: The homodimeric channel's symmetric, dual-topology structure demands that the pores adopt antiparallel orientations and that the two chemically distinct F− ions in one pore, designated F1− and F2−, are mirrored symmetrically in the other.
evidence: This is based on the structural symmetry observed in crystal structures.

claim: In each pore, the two ions are coordinated by dipolar H-bond donors situated along a transmembrane 'polar track'.
source: In each pore, the two ions are coordinated by dipolar H-bond donors situated along a transmembrane 'polar track' (Figure 1b) that constitutes a possible ion pathway through the channel.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The polar track constitutes a possible ion pathway through the channel.
source: In each pore, the two ions are coordinated by dipolar H-bond donors situated along a transmembrane 'polar track' (Figure 1b) that constitutes a possible ion pathway through the channel.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural arrangement of the polar track.

claim: The F− coordination shells are completed by conserved phenylalanine residues interacting edge-on with the bound anions.
source: Moreover, the F− coordination shells are completed by conserved phenylalanine residues interacting edge-on with the bound anions (Figure 1b), Phe80 associated with the F1− pair and Phe83 with the F2− pair.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Phe80 is associated with the F1− pair.
source: Moreover, the F− coordination shells are completed by conserved phenylalanine residues interacting edge-on with the bound anions (Figure 1b), Phe80 associated with the F1− pair and Phe83 with the F2− pair.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure.

claim: Phe83 is associated with the F2− pair.
source: Moreover, the F− coordination shells are completed by conserved phenylalanine residues interacting edge-on with the bound anions (Figure 1b), Phe80 associated with the F1− pair and Phe83 with the F2− pair.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure.

claim: These four aromatic side chains adopt a striking side-to-face 'Phe-box' arrangement.
source: These four aromatic side chains adopt a striking side-to-face 'Phe-box' arrangement that supports an unusual aromatic-halide coordination motif proposed to be essential for F−-specific binding and permeation (Stockbridge et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure and prior analysis.

claim: The Phe-box arrangement supports an unusual aromatic-halide coordination motif proposed to be essential for F−-specific binding and permeation.
source: These four aromatic side chains adopt a striking side-to-face 'Phe-box' arrangement that supports an unusual aromatic-halide coordination motif proposed to be essential for F−-specific binding and permeation (Stockbridge et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: Edge-on aromatic-anion coordination geometry makes chemical sense in light of the electropositive hydrogens of the quadrupolar aromatic ring.
source: Edge-on aromatic-anion coordination geometry makes chemical sense in light of the electropositive hydrogens of the quadrupolar aromatic ring (Jackson et al., 2007; Philip et al., 2011; Schwans et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to chemical studies on aromatic-anion interactions.

claim: The two antiparallel polar tracks and their associated bound F− ions are well-separated in the crystal structure, with no plausible pathway for ions to transfer between tracks.
source: The two antiparallel polar tracks and their associated bound F− ions are well-separated in the crystal structure, with no plausible pathway for ions to transfer between tracks.
evidence: This is an observation from the crystal structure.

claim: These structural features led to the proposal that the two polar tracks represent two separate pores.
source: These structural features led to the proposal, to be tested here, that the two polar tracks represent two separate pores.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural observations.

claim: Mutation of the conserved Phe-box residues in a Fluc homologue from B. pertussis was previously shown to severely inhibit F− transport.
source: Mutation of the conserved Phe-box residues in a Fluc homologue from B. pertussis was previously shown to severely inhibit F− transport, an effect presumed to reflect the replacement of F−-friendly binding sites in the conduction pathways with kinetic barriers to ion movement (Stockbridge et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The inhibitory effect of Phe-box mutations is presumed to reflect the replacement of F−-friendly binding sites in the conduction pathways with kinetic barriers to ion movement.
source: Mutation of the conserved Phe-box residues in a Fluc homologue from B. pertussis was previously shown to severely inhibit F− transport, an effect presumed to reflect the replacement of F−-friendly binding sites in the conduction pathways with kinetic barriers to ion movement (Stockbridge et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis about the effect of the mutations.

claim: Crystal structures of F80I and F83I Ec2 mutants were solved.
source: This idea is now tested in Ec2, where we here examine occupancy of the F−-binding sites by solving crystal structures of Phe-box mutants F80I and F83I (Figure 1c, Table 1) and assessing their transport function.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 1c and Table 1.

claim: Substitution of each aromatic side chain by Ile specifically extinguishes the corresponding pair of F− densities, one in each pore, while leaving the other pair Phe-coordinated and unperturbed.
source: Substitution of each aromatic side chain by Ile specifically extinguishes the corresponding pair of F− densities, one in each pore, while leaving the other pair Phe-coordinated and unperturbed.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structures shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The mutations cause only local structural disturbances such as alternate rotamers at nearby sidechains Ser84 and Ser110.
source: The mutations cause only local structural disturbances such as alternate rotamers at nearby sidechains Ser84 and Ser110 (Cα rmsd 0.4 Å, 0.2 Å for F80I, F83I).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison of mutant and WT structures.

claim: F80I and F83I mutations reduce F− flux in reconstituted liposomes to undetectable levels.
source: Functionally, the mutations are dramatic, reducing F− flux in reconstituted liposomes to undetectable levels (Figure 1d), a >104-fold rate inhibition compared to the wildtype (WT) channel (Stockbridge et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the flux data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: F80I and F83I mutations cause a >10^4-fold rate inhibition compared to the wildtype channel.
source: Functionally, the mutations are dramatic, reducing F− flux in reconstituted liposomes to undetectable levels (Figure 1d), a >104-fold rate inhibition compared to the wildtype (WT) channel (Stockbridge et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of flux data with prior WT measurements.

claim: Phe80 and Phe83 lie along F− permeation pathways.
source: These facts imply that Phe80 and Phe83 lie along F− permeation pathways and that the functional defect in the mutants stems directly from the loss of the aromatic ring as a F−-binding partner in these pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and functional data on the mutants.

claim: The functional defect in the mutants stems directly from the loss of the aromatic ring as a F−-binding partner in these pathways.
source: These facts imply that Phe80 and Phe83 lie along F− permeation pathways and that the functional defect in the mutants stems directly from the loss of the aromatic ring as a F−-binding partner in these pathways.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference from the structural and functional data.

claim: A tandem dimer was constructed by connecting two copies of the WT Ec2 sequence with a linker containing a foreign transmembrane helix to force an antiparallel arrangement of the two domains.
source: We therefore constructed a tandem dimer by connecting two copies of the WT Ec2 sequence with a linker containing a foreign transmembrane helix to force an antiparallel arrangement of the two domains (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental construct, supported by figures.

claim: The tandem dimer construct is denoted 'WT/WT'.
source: This construct, denoted 'WT/WT', mimics eukaryotic Fluc genes (Smith et al., 2015; Stockbridge et al., 2013), and it reprises an engineered homologue previously used to infer dual-topology assembly of Fluc channels (Stockbridge et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a naming convention for the construct.

claim: The WT/WT construct mimics eukaryotic Fluc genes.
source: This construct, denoted 'WT/WT', mimics eukaryotic Fluc genes (Smith et al., 2015; Stockbridge et al., 2013), and it reprises an engineered homologue previously used to infer dual-topology assembly of Fluc channels (Stockbridge et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on eukaryotic Fluc genes.

claim: The WT/WT construct reprises an engineered homologue previously used to infer dual-topology assembly of Fluc channels.
source: This construct, denoted 'WT/WT', mimics eukaryotic Fluc genes (Smith et al., 2015; Stockbridge et al., 2013), and it reprises an engineered homologue previously used to infer dual-topology assembly of Fluc channels (Stockbridge et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The concatemer expresses poorly (~40 μg/L culture).
source: The concatemer expresses poorly (~40 μg/L culture), but well enough for purification and reconstitution in liposomes and planar lipid bilayers (Figure 2b–d).
evidence: This is an observation from the expression experiments.

claim: The concatemer is functionally indistinguishable from the homodimeric WT channel with respect to unitary current, high intrinsic open probability, brief, infrequent closings, F− selectivity, and submicromolar affinity block by monobody proteins.
source: The concatemer is functionally indistinguishable from the homodimeric WT channel with respect to unitary current, high intrinsic open probability, brief, infrequent closings, F− selectivity, and submicromolar affinity block by monobody proteins (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is supported by functional data shown in the figure supplements.

claim: The F80I / F80I and F83I / F83I double mutants with identical Phe substitutions in both domains are inactive.
source: Moreover, the F80I / F80I and F83I / F83I double mutants with identical Phe substitutions in both domains - mimics of the mutant homodimers above - are likewise inactive (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by the flux data in Figure 2c.

claim: Concatemeric Ec2 faithfully recapitulates the behavior of the corresponding homodimers.
source: Concatemeric Ec2 thus faithfully recapitulates the behavior of the corresponding homodimers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the functional comparison of concatemers and homodimers.

claim: All four single Phe mutants, each of which leaves one pore unaltered, score active in efflux experiments.
source: The flux behavior of the Phe-box mutants in the fused-domain channels meet all expectations of two-pore assembly, as Figure 3 illustrates. All four single Phe mutants, each of which leaves one pore unaltered, score active in these efflux experiments (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by the flux data in Figure 3a.

claim: The two Phe residues from the same domain contribute to different pores.
source: Since the two Phe residues from the same domain contribute to different pores, and thus each pore harbors Phe80 from one domain and Phe83 from the other, we can distinguish two classes of double mutants: trans, wherein the two mutations reside in different pores, or cis, with both mutations in the same pore.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural arrangement of the Phe residues in the dual-topology dimer.

claim: Each pore harbors Phe80 from one domain and Phe83 from the other.
source: Since the two Phe residues from the same domain contribute to different pores, and thus each pore harbors Phe80 from one domain and Phe83 from the other, we can distinguish two classes of double mutants: trans, wherein the two mutations reside in different pores, or cis, with both mutations in the same pore.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural arrangement.

claim: Two trans double mutants, F80I / F80I and F83I / F83I, are completely inactive.
source: Two trans double mutants, F80I / F80I and F83I / F83I, are completely inactive, as shown above, while both cis double mutants (F80I / F83I, F83I / F80I) retain channel activity.
evidence: This is supported by the flux data in Figure 2c and Figure 3b.

claim: Both cis double mutants (F80I / F83I, F83I / F80I) retain channel activity.
source: Two trans double mutants, F80I / F80I and F83I / F83I, are completely inactive, as shown above, while both cis double mutants (F80I / F83I, F83I / F80I) retain channel activity.
evidence: This is supported by the flux data in Figure 3b.

claim: Channels with both pathways mutated are inactive irrespective of the particular combination of mutations.
source: These results show that channels with both pathways mutated are inactive irrespective of the particular combination of mutations, while those mutated in only one pathway remain active, as expected for two-pore construction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the flux data on double mutants.

claim: Channels mutated in only one pathway remain active, as expected for two-pore construction.
source: These results show that channels with both pathways mutated are inactive irrespective of the particular combination of mutations, while those mutated in only one pathway remain active, as expected for two-pore construction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the flux data, supporting the two-pore model.

claim: All single Phe-box mutants show unitary conductance of 5.7 ± 0.3 pS, roughly half that of WT/WT fused-domain or WT homodimeric channels (10.6 ± 0.1 pS).
source: The results (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) are unambiguous: all single Phe-box mutants show unitary conductance of 5.7 + 0.3 pS, roughly half that of WT/WT fused-domain or WT homodimeric channels (10.6 + 0.1 pS).
evidence: This is supported by single-channel recording data in Figure 4.

claim: The single-pore channels all recapitulate the high open probability and monobody block of WT.
source: Moreover, the single-pore channels all recapitulate the high open probability, and monobody block of WT.
evidence: This is supported by single-channel recording data.

claim: The cis double mutants show clear single-channel conductance that is lower (2.3 ± 0.2 pS) than the single mutants.
source: We additionally note that the cis double mutants also show clear single-channel conductance that is nonetheless lower (2.3 + 0.2 pS) than the single mutants, possibly due to subtle, non-local structural disturbance of the conducting pore arising from the double mutation in the inactive pore.
evidence: This is supported by single-channel recording data in Figure 4.

claim: The lower conductance of cis double mutants is possibly due to subtle, non-local structural disturbance of the conducting pore arising from the double mutation in the inactive pore.
source: We additionally note that the cis double mutants also show clear single-channel conductance that is nonetheless lower (2.3 + 0.2 pS) than the single mutants, possibly due to subtle, non-local structural disturbance of the conducting pore arising from the double mutation in the inactive pore.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed conductance difference.

claim: The ~2.5-fold drop in conductance of cis double mutants pales in comparison to the >10^4-fold drop observed when adding a second mutation in the trans configuration.
source: This ~2.5-fold drop in conductance, however, pales in comparison to the >104-fold drop observed when adding a second mutation in the trans configuration (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a comparison of the effects of cis vs trans double mutations.

claim: These experiments firmly establish the two-pore architecture suggested by crystal structures.
source: By examining the behavior of the Fluc Ec2 channel at a mechanistic level, these experiments now firmly establish the two-pore architecture suggested by crystal structures.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Two-pore architecture is a property of the entire Fluc family.
source: We consider this to be a property of the entire Fluc family, a conclusion further supported by indications of genetic drift in non-symmetric Flucs and the asymmetrical effects of mutations in yeast Fluc channels (Smith et al., 2015; Stockbridge et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a generalization supported by citations to studies on other Fluc homologues.

claim: The results highlight the importance of the conserved Phe-box residues in crafting coordination spheres for which F− ions are willing to shed their extensive aqueous hydration shells and enter the water-depleted confines of the ion-conduction pathway.
source: The results also highlight the importance of the conserved Phe-box residues in crafting coordination spheres for which F− ions are willing to shed their extensive aqueous hydration shells and enter the water-depleted confines of the ion-conduction pathway.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the functional importance of the Phe residues.

claim: WT Ec2 channels show infrequent, brief excursions to a substate of ~6 pS, approximately one-half the conductance of the open channel.
source: First, WT Ec2 channels show infrequent, brief excursions to a substate of ~6 pS, approximately one-half the conductance of the open channel (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by single-channel recording data in Figure 2d.

claim: It is natural to envision the substates as full closings of a single pore in a two-pore complex.
source: It is natural to envision these as full closings of a single pore in a two-pore complex (Stockbridge et al., 2013), a picture demanding that such partial closings be absent in the single-pore mutants.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the origin of the substates.

claim: The hypothesis that substates represent full closings of a single pore is contradicted by the kinetically similar substates of ~3 pS appearing in the single-pore mutants.
source: However, this idea is plainly contradicted by the kinetically similar substates of ~3 pS appearing in the single-pore mutants here (Figure 4a,c).
evidence: This is supported by single-channel data in Figure 4.

claim: The substates in both wildtype and mutant channels must reflect a rare conformation that acts simultaneously on both pores to reduce F− current in each.
source: Instead, the substates in both wildtype and mutant channels must reflect a rare conformation that acts simultaneously on both pores to reduce F− current in each, perhaps occurring in the wide, water-filled vestibules on the two ends of the channel complex.
evidence: This is a revised hypothesis based on the substate data from single-pore mutants.

claim: The substates perhaps occur in the wide, water-filled vestibules on the two ends of the channel complex.
source: Instead, the substates in both wildtype and mutant channels must reflect a rare conformation that acts simultaneously on both pores to reduce F− current in each, perhaps occurring in the wide, water-filled vestibules on the two ends of the channel complex.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion about the location of the conformational change.

claim: The edge-to-face arrangement of the Phe-box in the WT channel had originally suggested that these four sidechains mutually stabilize and orient each other so as to properly coordinate the F− ions.
source: Second, the striking and aesthetically appealing edge-to-face arrangement of the Phe-box in the WT channel had originally suggested to us that these four sidechains mutually stabilize and orient each other so as to properly coordinate the F− ions (Stockbridge et al., 2015).
evidence: This was a prior hypothesis based on the WT structure.

claim: The Phe-mutant crystal structures refute the idea of a mutually stabilizing quartet, since the two Phe side chains remaining in each Ile substitution adopt identical orientations and crystallographic order as in the full Phe-box of WT.
source: However, the Phe-mutant crystal structures here, while validating F− coordination by the aromatic rings, refute the idea of a mutually stabilizing quartet, since the two Phe side chains remaining in each Ile substitution, though distant from each other, adopt identical orientations and crystallographic order as in the full Phe-box of WT (side chain rmsd 0.2 Å upon backbone alignment).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of mutant and WT crystal structures.

claim: The detailed trajectories of the two pores remain uncertain due to their very narrow bore.
source: Finally, despite the well-defined locations of the F− ions and the span of the polar track residues, we acknowledge that the detailed trajectories of the two pores remain uncertain due to their very narrow bore.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in the structural data.

claim: It is likely that the pores originate and end in the two aqueous vestibules that give the channel a symmetrical hourglass shape.
source: However, as indicated in the conjectural cartoon of Figure 5, it is likely that the pores originate and end in the two aqueous vestibules that give the channel a symmetrical hourglass shape.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the pore trajectories, illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: This suggestion follows from monobody interaction with Fluc channels.
source: This suggestion follows from monobody interaction with Fluc channels.
evidence: This is a rationale for the hypothesis about pore trajectories.

claim: In crystal structures of both Fluc homologues, monobodies cap and intrude into the vestibules with long loops bearing their diversified sequences.
source: In crystal structures of both Fluc homologues, monobodies cap and intrude into the vestibules with long loops bearing their diversified sequences (Stockbridge et al., 2015); in channel recordings here, the S9 monobody inhibits both double- and single-pore channels fully to the zero-current level, as though both pores are occluded simultaneously by the blocker.
evidence: This is supported by prior crystal structures and functional data in the current study.

claim: The S9 monobody inhibits both double- and single-pore channels fully to the zero-current level, as though both pores are occluded simultaneously by the blocker.
source: In crystal structures of both Fluc homologues, monobodies cap and intrude into the vestibules with long loops bearing their diversified sequences (Stockbridge et al., 2015); in channel recordings here, the S9 monobody inhibits both double- and single-pore channels fully to the zero-current level, as though both pores are occluded simultaneously by the blocker.
evidence: This is supported by single-channel recording data showing complete block.

claim: The vestibules are envisioned as common regions of low selectivity from which F− ions gain access to the separate F−-specific pathways.
source: This proposal thus envisions the vestibules as common regions of low selectivity from which F− ions gain access to the separate F−-specific pathways.
